analysis.one_liner: Bars federal pensions and benefits for ex-lawmakers and senior staff who become lobbyists.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committees but received no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take away federal retirement, health, and life insurance benefits from former Members of Congress and senior congressional staff if they go on to work as registered lobbyists — the "revolving door" between Capitol Hill and lobbying firms. It only applied to people who left Congress after the bill became law, and it did not touch money already saved in their retirement accounts. The bill was introduced in April 2023, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or even a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, in the form of a modest accountability measure: anyone who leaves Congress and immediately cashes in on their connections as a lobbyist would lose the federal pension and health benefits built up through their public service. Taxpayers indirectly benefit from a smaller incentive to trade public service for a lobbying career.

how_it_helps.text: It bars federal retirement, health, dental, vision, and life insurance benefits for any former Member or senior congressional employee who later works and is compensated as a registered lobbyist.
It applies prospectively only, to people who leave Congress after enactment, so it does not strip benefits anyone already has.

analysis.who_pays: Former Members and senior congressional staff who choose a lobbying career after leaving office — they would forgo federal retirement and health benefits for months while working as lobbyists. Lobbying firms would have a slightly harder recruiting pitch for former lawmakers.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition only applies while a former Member or senior staffer is employed and compensated as a registered lobbyist; once they stop lobbying, benefits eligibility appears to resume, so the deterrent is narrow.

Members retain their nonforfeitable Thrift Savings Plan balances and lump-sum credits, so the bill bars ongoing federal benefits but not the retirement savings already accrued during congressional service.

It applies only to former Members and senior staff who go through the formal lobbying registration system; work as a 'strategic adviser' or in-house government-relations executive that falls below registration thresholds would not trigger the bar.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea is modest and well-aimed: if congressional service is a stepping stone to a lobbying career, the pension should not follow. The bill's real limit is that a Member could simply wait out the brief window in which they are compensated as a registered lobbyist before collecting benefits, and it would not stop the revolving door itself — only make it slightly less comfortable. It was never debated or amended, so no formal cost analysis exists; the direct cost is essentially zero, and the honest objection is that the provision is narrow and easy to structure around.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, neither of which acted on it, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended and all work on it expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Posey introduced the bill on April 6, 2023, and it was referred to the House Administration and Oversight and Accountability Committees.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, including none from either party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and senior staff considering lobbying careers keep the option of collecting federal pensions and health benefits while lobbying, because the bill never advanced. The lobbying industry faces no added cost.

for.name: Rep. Bill Posey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it in the House; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Oversight and Accountability
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: Lobbying firms value hires who bring congressional relationships and pension security; the bill would cut off the federal benefits side of the package for former lawmakers and senior staff. The lobbying industry actively opposed similar proposals in past Congresses, though this bill drew no recorded action.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: The bill makes a post-Congress lobbying career carry a personal pension and health-benefits cost, changing the calculus for those weighing a lobbying job after leaving office.
